text: The shared fridge at work hadn't been cleaned in months. When I opened the crisper drawer, a brown slick of liquid and something furry looked back at me. The smell was revolting, so I left my salad on the counter and ate lunch at my desk instead.

The restroom at the bus depot had a sticky floor, an empty soap dispenser, and a mop bucket full of grey water. I touched nothing I didn't have to. It was filthy and honestly repulsive, and I washed my hands twice at the café down the road before ordering anything.

While packing up my rented flat, I pulled a long slimy clump of hair out of the shower drain. It was so gross that I dropped it into the bin with two fingers and turned my face away. I scrubbed my hands under hot water for a full minute, still grimacing at the memory.

At the night market, I watched the vendor wipe his nose on his wrist and then pick up the dumplings with bare hands. It was disgusting to see. I put my wallet away, walked past the next three stalls, and bought a packaged biscuit from a shop instead.

I found a carton of milk that had been sitting in my gym bag since Saturday. When I unscrewed the cap, the sour, curdled smell hit me and I nearly gagged. It was revolting, and I carried the whole bag outside at arm's length before dealing with it.

The communal shower at the hostel had black mold creeping along the curtain and a pile of damp, tangled towels in the corner. Something about the slimy tiles under my feet made me recoil. I found it vile and rinsed off in under a minute with my flip-flops on.

After a week away, I lifted the lid of the kitchen bin and saw maggots writhing across the potato peels. The sight was so repulsive that I let the lid drop with a clang. I tied the bag shut with a towel over my nose and carried it down four flights of stairs.

The hotel sheets had a yellowish stain near the pillow and a few stray hairs that were definitely not mine. I stripped the bed down to the mattress and found even more grime there. It was nasty, so I slept on top of my own jacket and a towel.

My train seat was tacky with something spilled, and the whole carriage smelled of stale sweat and old fried food. I stood by the door for the entire ride, thinking how revolting the place was. The window wouldn't open, so I watched the stations slide past until my stop.

Cleaning out the pantry, I tore open a bag of flour and found pale larvae and sticky webbing woven through it. I felt thoroughly repulsed. I threw the bag out, wiped every shelf with vinegar, and still caught myself shuddering at the sight of a rice packet.

At the public pool this morning, a used bandage drifted past my elbow, grey and waterlogged. The sight made my stomach turn, and I climbed out right away. I sat on the bench in my towel, trying to shake the image while the lifeguard finished his tea.

Bin day went badly: a garbage bag split on the pavement outside my gate, spilling rotten fish heads and slimy tea leaves everywhere. The smell was foul and the liquid was oozing toward my doorstep. I held my breath and swept it aside, thinking how disgusting it all was.

At the potluck, the serving spoon in the curry had a crust of dried gravy and a crumb of something orange stuck to the handle. I looked at it and felt revolted, so I took only rice and papad. Someone asked if I wasn't hungry, and I just smiled and said I'd eaten earlier.

I read an exposé about a garment factory that charges its workers for their uniforms and then fines them for taking toilet breaks. The whole arrangement struck me as vile. I closed the tab, made a cup of tea, and kept turning over how anyone could build a profit on that.

Outside the market, I saw a man laugh while he poked a stick at a stray dog's ribs, just for fun. The casual cruelty of it made me feel morally sick. I bought my vegetables and left, still unable to shake how repulsive his amusement was.

A colleague at lunch bragged about talking elderly customers into warranties they would never need, calling them easy marks. I looked at my plate and felt a deep revulsion at him. His grin as he described it was repellent, and I changed seats before dessert.

I watched a documentary about puppy mills last night, where the animals were treated like inventory and thrown away when they stopped being profitable. I found it deeply repugnant. I switched it off halfway, made a cup of chamomile, and kept feeling revolted that people can think that way.

Someone in a classmates' group chat shared a photo of a drunk girl passed out on a sofa, and a dozen people piled on with jokes. I felt revulsion at how degrading it was. I muted the chat and went back to folding laundry, still wrinkling my nose at the whole thing.

The man at the café table next to mine described his tenants as livestock who should be grateful for whatever he gave them. I found his attitude repugnant, almost grimy somehow. I finished my coffee quickly and left without looking at him again.

On the metro, a man flung coins at a young ticket attendant's face and laughed as she picked them off the floor. The way he treated her was degrading and honestly revolting to witness. I stared at the route map until my stop came.

A friend sent me a link about influencers who stage photos with hungry children, paying them to look miserable for donations. I felt revolted by the exploitation. It seemed so slimy and calculated that I unfollowed three accounts, then went to put the kettle on.

At the farm stall, the owner proudly showed me how he keeps his calves in tiny dark crates to make the meat paler. I felt a wave of moral revulsion and could not look at the display of cutlets. I bought nothing, thanked him politely, and drove home with the radio off.

A news report described a gang selling fake medicine to the families of terminally ill patients, complete with fancy labels and false promises. It was so foul that my skin crawled just reading it. I read the article twice and then switched to a recipe blog to clear my head.

At the office party, a senior director cornered two interns and kept making crude jokes about their looks while they smiled stiffly. His behaviour was sleazy and repulsive. I walked to the snack table, picked at a samosa, and kept my back to him.

I read that some traders hoarded drinking water during the floods and sold it at triple the price. It's an ugly, repulsive way to behave, preying on people's desperation. I put my phone face down and went to water the plants on the balcony, still feeling morally sickened.

The internet company cancelled my installation appointment for the third time, and I had taken another day off work to wait. I was angry the moment the call came in. I kept my voice level, took notes, and then slammed the cupboard door harder than I needed to.

My manager moved the report deadline up by two days and told us in the corridor, as if it were nothing. I'm angry that nobody asked whether the new date was even possible. I typed three replies, deleted them all, and reorganised my desk drawer instead.

Someone has parked across my driveway for the fourth morning this week, and I had to wait twenty minutes for them to move. I'm fed up and angry that nobody respects such a simple rule. I wrote a note, stuck it on the windscreen, and pressed the tape down hard.

My brother took my bicycle without asking and returned it with a bent wheel and no apology. I'm really angry about it, since he knows how carefully I save for anything I own. I told him so at dinner, and he shrugged while I passed the dal.

The airline lost my suitcase for the second time this year, and the desk clerk just pointed to a form. I was furious standing there in yesterday's clothes. I filled out every line in block capitals, pressing so hard that the pen nearly went through the paper.

I came home and found the landlord had let himself into my flat to check the geyser, without any message or notice. It's my space, and I'm angry that he doesn't see that. I put the kettle on, wrote an email citing the rental agreement, and sent it before dinner.

At today's meeting, my teammate presented my analysis as his own and nobody corrected him. I sat there with my jaw tight, angry at being erased. Afterwards I sent the original file to everyone with the timestamp attached and went for a walk around the block.

The bank charged me the same fee twice, and after forty minutes on hold the agent told me that was normal. I'm so angry about being treated as if I were stupid. I took screenshots, requested a written reply, and drank my tea standing at the counter.

I discovered my sister has been reading my private notebook, because she quoted a line back to me at lunch. I'm angry that she crossed that boundary. I moved the notebook into my bag, told her it was off limits, and went to my room to study.

The courier left my parcel in the rain on the doorstep for the third time, even though the instructions clearly said to ring the bell. I'm fed up and angry. I carried the damp box inside, took a photo for the complaint form, and sent it off.

The promotion went to a man who joined the team last month, even though I trained him and covered his tasks. I'm angry about how unfair that is. I sat quietly through the announcement, then went to the stairwell and gripped the rail until my hands stopped shaking.

Construction has started at six every morning outside my window, and the notice on the gate promised quiet hours that nobody follows. I'm furious at being treated as if my sleep doesn't matter. I made coffee, stood glaring at the crane, and rang the site office again.

At the family gathering, my aunt once again waved away my job in front of everyone and asked when I'd get a real one. I felt anger rise as the others laughed along. I answered shortly, kept my hands busy with the plates, and left before the cake.

The online store promised a refund within three days, and it's now been three weeks of automated replies. I'm angry that they keep dodging the issue. I opened another ticket, pasted in the earlier emails, and set a reminder to phone them tomorrow morning.

My colleague keeps booking meetings over my lunch hour, even after I told him twice that I need that break. I'm angry that he ignores it. I declined the invite, wrote a short, firm note, and ate my rice at my desk with the door closed.

My flight to Lisbon leaves on Tuesday, and I've already checked my passport three times. Tonight I read about the tram routes and the neighbourhood where I'll be staying. I keep counting the days and wondering what the streets will look like when I step out of the airport.

The community garden opens for the new season on Saturday. I sorted my seed packets into labelled envelopes and keep wondering which bed I'll be assigned. I'm curious about the other members and eager to start digging in the soil.

Next week I'm meeting the architect to see the plans for the new library branch. I've been reading about the site and jotting down questions in my notebook. I'm really curious how the reading room will be laid out and what they'll say about the schedule.

On Friday I'm finally seeing a band I've listened to for ten years. I've been scanning their old setlists and thinking about which songs they might play. I even picked out which shirt to wear, and I'm eager for the evening to arrive.

We get the keys to the new flat in a month, and I've started measuring the rooms with a tape. I wonder how the morning light will fall across the kitchen. My head is full of questions about the neighbourhood and where the nearest bakery might be.

The cooking class on Sunday focuses on regional breads, and I've been reading about the techniques all week. I'm very keen to see how the instructor handles the dough. I bought a new apron and cleared space on the shelf for a proofing basket.

Race day is in two weeks. I laid out my shoes, bib, and hydration belt on the bed tonight and studied the route map. I'm eager to see the course in person and to find out how the final kilometre feels.

My new camera lens is on its way, and I've been refreshing the tracking page whenever I make tea. It should arrive by Thursday. I'm curious what the first shots will look like at dusk, and I've already planned a walk by the river.

We're hiking up to the ridge next weekend. I spent the evening spreading the map on the floor and tracing the trail, wondering how the sunrise will look from the top. I'm looking forward to the early start and that first view.

My book club hosts the author of our current novel on Thursday. I've almost finished the last chapters and wrote down questions on index cards. I'm genuinely looking forward to hearing how she answers them and what the rest of the room will ask.

My friend's wedding is next month, and I just bought a new tie. I keep thinking about the venue, the music, and the dancing I've heard goes on past midnight. I'm looking forward to seeing how the whole day unfolds.
The pottery workshop begins on Thursday. I bought an apron and watched a video about centring clay. I wonder what I'll end up making, a bowl or a lopsided cup, and I'm eager to find out.

A meteor shower peaks around three tomorrow night, so I set an alarm and checked the cloud forecast twice. I packed a flask, a blanket, and a star chart. I'm eager to see how many streaks I can spot from the roof.

The league's opening match is this Saturday, and I've been reading through the fixtures and the new squads. I'm planning to watch at Arjun's place with snacks. I'm curious how the new signings will fit in and what formation they'll try.

Tomorrow I take the early train to the hill town for the lantern festival. I've read about the procession and which lane has the best view. I'm eager to see how it all unfolds, and I put my camera battery on the charger overnight.

Mum was humming as she chopped onions this evening, flour on her sleeve and the radio turned low. I stood in the doorway and felt a rush of tenderness for her. I wanted to wrap my arms around her, so I did, and she told me to mind the knife.

Dad's old reading glasses were lying on the table next to the crossword. I picked them up and felt a warm tug of affection for him. I'm going to call him tomorrow and ask about the one clue he never manages to finish.

Rahul fell asleep on the couch with his book still open on his chest. I covered him with a blanket and stood there longer than I needed to. I adore the way he frowns in his sleep, and I wanted to stay close until he woke.

My best friend and I have lived in different cities for two years now. Tonight I scrolled through our old photos and found myself smiling at her ridiculous haircut. I love her deeply, and I want to sit across from her again with chai and nothing to do.

I sat on the verandah with my grandmother while she peeled peas into a steel bowl. I looked at her hands, so soft and creased, and felt deeply attached to her. I stayed there past sunset just to be near her.

My little sister was drawing at the dining table, tongue poking out, colouring in a cat with purple fur. I'm so fond of her. I leaned over, tucked her hair behind her ear, and asked if I could keep the drawing for my wall.

From across the kitchen I heard Meera laugh at something on her phone, and I realised how much I love that sound. I put my pan down and just watched her for a second. I want to stay close to her, in the same room, for as long as possible.

A postcard from my old friend Tom arrived today, with a drawing of a one-eyed cat on the back. I stuck it on the fridge. I care about him so much, and I'm already planning to write back with a drawing of my own.

My brother was belting out a song in the shower again, completely out of tune. I leaned on the wall outside the door and listened. I feel so affectionate toward him, even when he's being ridiculous, and I wouldn't trade him for anyone.

I held my niece's small hand while we crossed the street to the bakery. Her fingers were warm and sticky from the sweet she'd been eating. I felt such tenderness for her and just wanted to look after her always.
My husband has been away at a work site for ten days, and his old sweatshirt was still draped over the chair. I folded it and set it on the bed. I love him, and I want him close again.

My friend and I have been sitting on her balcony every Sunday for years, trading bad jokes over a pot of tea. This evening I realised how fond I am of her. She's become part of my life, and I'd like to keep this ritual going.

My cousin visits each summer and sleeps in the room next to mine. This morning I made her favourite breakfast without thinking, just because I wanted her to feel looked after. I love having her near, and the house feels fuller when she's around.

I wrote a short anniversary note to Anika and left it under her coffee mug. I wrote that I love her and that I want to keep growing old beside her. I felt shy and tender as I propped it up and went to have a shower.

Dad taught me chess on the old wooden board again tonight, moving his bishop slowly so I could follow. I cherish these evenings with him. I love how patient he is with me, and I want to keep him close for as many games as we get.

I expected to feel sad when I handed in my keys at the old office, but I didn't. I signed the form, walked to the bus stop, and bought a tea from the cart on the corner. It was an ordinary Thursday afternoon.

I'm not angry about the schedule change. The class moved to Thursday, so I updated my calendar, emailed my study partner, and rearranged my laundry day. Everything else stayed the same, and I had dal and rice for dinner.

I never felt nervous before the dentist today. It was only a routine cleaning, thirty minutes in the chair, and then I picked up bread and eggs on the way home. The receptionist gave me a new toothbrush in a paper bag.
Although everyone had told me the film would make me cry, it didn't. I watched it to the end, ate most of the popcorn, and went to bed around eleven. In the morning I took the earlier bus.

I wasn't surprised when the meeting ran overtime, and I didn't mind. I sat in my usual seat, took notes on the third agenda item, and refilled my water bottle at the break. The rest of the day went as planned.

I'm not angry at Dev for cancelling the beach trip, and I told him so. What I feel is a heavy sadness that we won't sit on that sand together this year. I put the sunscreen back in the drawer and sat with the quiet for a while.

I expected to be frightened before my first flight, but I wasn't, not even when the plane lined up on the runway. What I felt was a bright, forward-leaning anticipation about seeing the coastline from above. I kept my eyes on the window.

I thought the audition would leave me crushed, and I was ready for sadness, but it never came. Walking out of the hall, I felt a wide, delighted joy just from having sung in front of the panel. I bought a samosa to celebrate on the way home.

I wasn't scared when the power went out for the third night, only angry. The electricity company promised repairs last week and nothing has changed. I'm irritated enough to write a formal complaint, and I lit the candles feeling stubbornly annoyed.

I wasn't surprised when Priya returned the borrowed money on the exact day she'd promised. She has never let me down, and I rely on her completely. I made her tea when she came by and didn't even count the notes.

I'm not angry about the transfer, but I feel a quiet sadness at leaving this street and its tea stall. Still, I believe the new job will open doors for me, and I think things will turn out well. I wrapped my mugs in newspaper and taped up the first box.

I never felt nervous at my sister's wedding. I was happy the whole evening, laughing with her friends, and I felt so much love for her as she walked in. I kept a sweet in my pocket for later and danced until my feet hurt.

I wasn't scared walking into the lab on my first day. Instead I was surprised at how bright and quiet it was, nothing like the dim basement I'd imagined, and I was eager for tomorrow's first experiment. I read the equipment manual by the window until closing.

I'm not sad about losing the contract. I'm angry at the way they informed me by email at midnight, and I'm pessimistic that the firm will ever treat freelancers any better. I closed the laptop and decided to stop expecting anything different from them.

I didn't feel anxious handing the shop keys to the new manager. I trust her judgement completely, and I expect the place to do well this winter. I showed her the till, the supplier list, and where the spare fuses live, then left without looking back.

Before my driving test I was frightened, sure I'd stall the car and embarrass myself in front of the examiner. When the instructor said I'd passed, I laughed out loud and felt pure happiness flood in. I called my mother from the car park, grinning like a child.

When I saw the dented car door in the parking lot this morning, I was furious at whoever had driven off without leaving a note. By the afternoon the anger had drained away and left only a heavy sadness about how careless people have become. I sat in the car with the keys in my lap.

I was startled when the lid of the second-hand lunch box popped open and a grey, fuzzy lump rolled out, a sandwich from months ago. A second later I felt pure disgust at the sour smell and dropped the whole thing into the bin.

I felt deeply sad when I closed the shop for the last time, because eighteen years of mornings had ended. By evening I felt hopeful, making a list of ideas for the next chapter and certain that something good was coming. The old sign is leaning in my hallway now.

All week I was looking forward to the town fair, reading the schedule and planning which stalls to visit. Then the rain started and the organisers hinted it might be cancelled, and by Friday I felt sure the whole weekend would be a washout. I put the schedule in a drawer.

I was angry with my brother for keeping the loan a secret from me, and I let it show in the hallway. Later he sat down and went through every figure with me, and I felt confident that he would never hide anything from me again. I made two cups of tea.

The morning of my cousin's farewell party I felt pure happiness, laughing over old photos and eating too much cake. When the taxi finally pulled away that evening, the happiness gave way to a hollow sadness. I stood at the gate waving until I couldn't see the lights.

When my daughter ran into the road after her ball, I felt sheer terror until I saw the car stop in time. Once I'd pulled her back into my arms, what I felt was a rush of fierce love and tenderness. I kept my hand on her hair all the way home.

I couldn't hide my disgust when I first tasted the mushy, grey boiled vegetables in the canteen, and I pushed the tray away. The next day the cook handed me a plate of freshly fried parathas, and I felt happy all through lunch. I even went back for seconds.

I was stunned when I opened the door and found my old friend standing there with a suitcase, three days earlier than we'd planned. A moment later I was hugging her and feeling such warm affection that I forgot to ask about her flight. We stayed up talking.

For two weeks I was looking forward to the first day at the new workshop, reading the syllabus and choosing my tools. But as the morning drew near, I felt a fluttering dread that I'd be the only beginner in the room. I checked my bag three times.

On the drive to the clinic I was convinced the test results would be bad and the next months would be miserable. Then the doctor said everything was clear, and I broke into a grin and felt light with happiness. I bought flowers on the way home.

I was fuming when the landlord raised the rent without warning and left a note on the door. After I read my agreement and found a clause protecting me, I started to feel hopeful that I could negotiate it back down. I called the housing office the next morning.

I felt a heavy sadness at the news that my friend was relocating, and I barely spoke at dinner. Later she promised to visit every second month and send updates, and I trusted her, since she has always kept her word. I helped her pack the books.

I was startled to find the old bakery on the corner shuttered with a notice on the door, because it had been there my whole life. As I stood reading the notice, my surprise turned into a quiet sadness for all those mornings. I walked on without buying bread.
